cells.tense: A seed is in your hands and you are tending it well.
cells.act: give a concrete piece of help and finish it
cells.ask: Where you're already helping something grow, give it what it needs this week and then bring your help to an end. Let the work finish. Ending it well is the ask.
cells.core:
Something real is in your hands, small and early, and the way you're helping it is right. You give what it needs without forcing it, and you can tell a hand steadying from a hand gripping. That's the whole craft of caring for what's growing, and you're inside it, not perfectly, but well enough.

The support you give is the ordinary kind — strength moving to where it's needed, then arriving. Give what's growing exactly what it needs this week, then stop. Not less than it needs, not more. Letting your part come to an end is where the practice lives. When you can finish helping a thing, it grows on what it has, and your hands come back to you.
cells.sheetLine: You're helping it the way it needs to be helped.
cells.verb: holding the first form of a thing you are tending
cells.place: beside what is growing, hands steady

cells.tense: You will have arranged everything before it has had a chance to begin.
cells.act: let the felt connection be complete
cells.ask: Sit with what you're growing for a few minutes this week — no adjusting, no fixing, no next step. Stay until everything you feel about it is there, then go on with your day.
cells.core:
The future is where the plans live right now — the schedule, the stage after this stage, the watering timed to the hour. You can already see the thing further along than it is, and you keep reaching ahead to meet it. The help has turned into steering: hands that were steadying have started doing the work, because standing in the open space where a seed is and not doing anything feels like leaving something undone.

What's thin is contact with the thing itself, not more care for its future. Sit with what you're growing for a few minutes — no adjusting, no next step — until everything you feel about it is there. Then it gets to be whatever it actually is, maybe at a pace you didn't plan. That sits you back down beside it instead of over it.
cells.sheetLine: You don't have to grow it before it grows.

cells.tense: You were handed something to tend, and you stopped arriving for it.
cells.act: see the true thing whole, as the last word on it
cells.ask: Take the thing you've been half-tending and lay all of it where you can see it at once — where it stands, what you did, what you didn't. Look until the picture holds, then leave it be.
cells.core:
Something was put in your hands — a responsibility, a person, a piece of work still early — and while it is still small, your care keeps not arriving. The help has been going on from a distance, and from where you stand the whole thing can look already too late to bother with. The care was not the problem. Seeing it clearly is what's missing, and without that the hours blur and nothing feels worth the hand.

So look at the whole of the small thing you've left halfway: where it stands, what you did and didn't do. When the whole picture holds, it's finished — you can close it, keep it, or start it properly from the state it's actually in. Seeing it complete is the whole ask. Nothing about it has to be pushed or felt into.
cells.sheetLine: Look at it whole before you look away.

cells.tense: The tending is happening by your hand and your word for it is luck.
cells.ask: On the way into one check-in with what you're growing, notice that you are doing the checking and deciding what it gets. Then do it exactly as you would have.
cells.core:
Under your hands something is being kept alive and moving — a small thing, early days, maybe a person or a piece of work. Asked about it, you'd say it's mostly running itself. But the timing, the small adjustments, the sense of when to step in and when to leave it alone — those come from you. You are helping it take form, and your part in that has no name in your account of it.

On the way into one check-in with what's growing, notice that you are doing the checking, that you are the one deciding what it gets. Then go ahead and do it exactly as you would have. The act doesn't change. Only the credit does. You aren't taking charge of something you were only borrowing — you are already the hand steadying it.
cells.sheetLine: The hand steadying it is yours. You just haven't signed.

attempts.check: The unsupported claim is that the person is standing in front of a seed that is theirs to plant — the record supports a beginning presenting itself, not that they asked for it or want it. A reader could reasonably say the tending is of other people's growth, not their own, and my read would still hold because the ask acts on whatever is being tended in front of them. The ask survives being wrong: it asks only that they look at the whole of the small thing they are already tending, before they arrange the next thing for it. The sentence that serves me more than them is the Too Much line about the other person's pace — I cut it, and I kept every claim on this side of the fence, naming only what a person could see themselves doing.
